**It’s not a bug – it’s the intended “local‑fonts” fallback that MapLibre GL JS has used since v5.11.0.**
When a style **doesn’t contain a `glyphs` field**, MapLibre GL JS treats every entry in `text‑font` exactly like a CSS `font‑family` list:
1. It looks for a **web‑font** that you have loaded with `@font-face` (or that the browser already knows about).
2. If it can’t find a matching web‑font, it falls back to the **system default font** for the platform (e.g. “Arial”, “Helvetica”, “sans‑serif”, etc.).
Because you haven’t supplied a glyph‑PBF server, the engine never asks for any `.pbf` files

column1: ## How to get the exact font you want
You have three practical options, depending on whether you want to keep the style completely offline, serve glyphs from a server, or rely on the browser’s font loading.
### 1️⃣ Load the font locally (the simplest fix for GL JS)
1. **Add a web‑font definition** somewhere that loads before you create the map:
2. **Make sure the name in `text-font` matches exactly** the `font-family` you declared:
3. **Optional – verify** with the browser dev‑tools → *Network* tab that the font file is being requested and loaded.
If the font loads successfully, MapLibre will render the labels with it, and you’ll no longer see the generic fallback.
### 2️⃣ Serve glyph PBFs (the classic MapLibre way)
If you prefer the original SDF‑glyph pipeline (or you need the same look on Native), do one of the following:

| **Standard font (Noto, Open Sans, Roboto, etc.)** | You can copy the pre‑built glyph tree from an existing server (e.g. `https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/`) to your own origin, or pull the ready‑made packages from <https://github.com/openmaptiles/fonts> or <https://github.com/UNDP-Data/fonts>. |

| **Custom brand font** | Generate the `.pbf` files yourself with **Font Maker** (`npm i -g @mapbox/font-maker`) or **fontnik**. The command is roughly:
`font-maker --font /path/to/MyFancyFont-Regular.ttf --output ./fonts`
which creates the `{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` hierarchy. |

| **Update the style** | Add a `glyphs` URL template that points at your host:
`""glyphs"": ""https://my.cdn.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf""` |
Now `text-font` will be resolved against the glyph server, and the same PBFs will be used by both GL JS and Native (provided you also set `font-faces` on Native, if you need offline).
### 3️⃣ Keep the style “glyph‑free” but control the fallback
If you like the convenience of the local‑fonts mode but want a specific system font (e.g. a better CJK face), you can set the map option `localIdeographFontFamily`:
localIdeographFontFamily: '""Noto Sans CJK SC"", ""Microsoft YaHei"", sans-serif'
- **CJK characters** will be drawn with the first available font in that list.
- **Non‑CJK scripts** still follow the normal `text-font` → web‑font → system fallback chain.
> **Do not set `localIdeographFontFamily: false`** unless you really need the exact glyph shapes from a server (it forces the engine to request PBFs for every ideograph, which is very slow).
## Common pitfalls & how to avoid them

| Labels appear, but **different weight** (e.g. regular instead of bold) | You only loaded the regular weight via `@font-face`. | Add separate `@font-face` rules for each weight (`font-weight: 700` etc.) and list them in `text-font` (e.g. `""My Fancy Font Bold""`). |

| Font loads locally **on desktop** but not on **mobile** | The font file is blocked by CORS or the mobile browser can’t fetch it (e.g. missing `crossorigin` attribute). | Serve the font with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain) and add `crossorigin=""anonymous""` to the `<link>`/`@font-face`. |

| Text disappears after a style reload | `glyphs` field was added later, causing the engine to switch back to the PBF path, but the server returns 404. | Either keep `glyphs` omitted **or** make sure the server serves the requested PBFs. |

| CJK characters look **tiny** or **pixelated** | `localIdeographFontFamily` is set to a font that isn’t installed on the device. | Use a font that is guaranteed to exist (e.g. the default `sans-serif`) or bundle a web‑font for CJK and set `localIdeographFontFamily` to that family name. |
| Arabic/Hebrew text is **reversed** or missing ligatures | RTL plugin not loaded. | `import { setRTLTextPlugin } from 'maplibre-gl'

It assumes you are using **MapLibre‑Native ≥ 11.13.0** (the first version that ships the `font‑faces` property) and that you want **zero network traffic** for text – i.e. no `glyphs` URL, no external glyph‑PBF server.

| Since 5.11 GL JS can fall back to TinySDF (local fonts) when a glyph PBF fails. | **Native has no automatic fallback** – you have to tell the engine which local font file covers which Unicode range. |
| `localIdeographFontFamily` handles CJK on‑device. | Same option exists (`localIdeographFontFamily`) but it only affects **CJK**

column1: **Short answer:** **No.** The `font‑faces` property is a **MapLibre Native‑only** feature. GL JS does not understand it, and copying the block into a GL JS style will be ignored (or will cause a validation error).
Below is a quick‑reference table, followed by the practical ways you can get *offline‑font* behavior in a GL JS web app, and why the two SDKs can’t share the same configuration today.
| Property | What it does | Where it lives |

| `font-faces` (style root) | Maps each name that appears in a layer’s `text-font` array to **one or more local font files** (TTF/OTF) **and** an explicit Unicode range for each file. | Only read by MapLibre Native (Android ≥ 11.13.0, iOS ≥ 6.18.0). |
| Goal | Offline rendering without a glyph‑server, with **exact control** over which file supplies which code‑points. |  |
GL JS has **no equivalent**. It either:
* **Falls back to the browser’s own font‑fallback mechanism** (available since GL JS 5.11.0) when `glyphs` is omitted or a particular glyph range fails to load.
## 2️⃣ Why you can’t just copy it
| **Spec mismatch** | The style spec for GL JS (MapLibre‑Style‑Spec v8) does **not** define a `font-faces` top‑level property. The validator will flag it as “unknown property”. |
| **Runtime implementation** | GL JS never looks at the filesystem
column2: it runs in a browser sandbox where it cannot read arbitrary local files. `font-faces` expects a file‑system path (`file:///…`) that simply does not exist in the web context. |

column1: | **Different rendering pipeline** | Native maps each code‑point to a glyph that you pre‑generated (or that the engine loads from the file you declared). GL JS either loads **SDF glyph PBFs** from a server **or** uses **TinySDF** to rasterise the glyphs from a *web font* that the browser has already loaded. There is no “Unicode‑range → file” table in GL JS. |

| **Cross‑platform consistency** | Because the two pipelines are different, even if GL JS could read the same JSON it would not know *which* file to use for a given range, nor would it be able to guarantee the same visual output as Native. |
> **Bottom line:** The `font-faces` block is ignored by GL JS. You must use one of the GL JS‑specific mechanisms described next.
## 3️⃣ How to get *offline* (or “no‑glyph‑server”) text in GL JS
1. **Remove the `glyphs` field** from the style (or set it to `null`).
2. **Add the fonts you need to the page** via standard CSS `@font-face` (or a `<link>` to a Google‑Fonts‑style URL).
3. **Reference those names in `text-font`** exactly as you declared them.
4. **(Optional) Pre‑load the fonts** so the map doesn’t flash invisible text while the browser fetches them:
| **Offline** | As long as the `.woff2` files are served from the same origin (or a CORS‑enabled CDN), the map works without any `glyphs` network calls. |
| **Fallback order** | GL JS treats `text-font` exactly like a CSS `font-family` list: it tries the first name, then the next, etc. |
| **Unicode‑range control** | You *cannot* declare per‑range files. If you need a separate file for CJK vs. Latin you must load **both** fonts
column2: the browser will pick the glyph that matches the code‑point. This is usually fine because the browser already knows the correct Unicode ranges for each font. |

column1: Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** for adding a hillshade layer that is driven by a **raster‑DEM** source in a MapLibre GL JS map.
Everything is plain JavaScript (no extra plugins) and works with any recent version of MapLibre GL JS (≥ 2.0, but the same code runs on 5.x as well).
## 1. Pick / host a DEM tile set
MapLibre can read any raster‑DEM that follows the **XYZ** (or **WMTS**) tiling scheme and returns a single‑band image where the pixel value encodes elevation (usually in meters).
| Provider | URL template | Elevation encoding | Notes |
| **MapLibre DEM** (open‑source) | `https://demotiles.maplibre.org/terrain/v1/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | 16‑bit unsigned integer (little‑endian) stored in the red + green channels | Free, good for demos |
| **OpenMapTiles Terrain** | `https://tiles.openmaptiles.org/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | Same 16‑bit format | Requires an API key for heavy use |
| **Your own GeoTIFF → XYZ** | `https://my‑tiles.example.com/dem/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | Whatever you encode (see § 2) | Must be CORS‑enabled |

> **Tip:** If you already have a GeoTIFF, you can turn it into XYZ tiles with tools like **gdal2tiles.py** (or the newer **gdal2tiles‑c**). Make sure you export the elevation as a **16‑bit unsigned integer** (the format MapLibre expects by default).
## 2. Add the raster‑DEM source to the style
style: 'https://demotiles.maplibre.org/style.json', // any base style you like
// 2️⃣  When the style is ready, add the DEM source
// The DEM is encoded as 16‑bit unsigned integer (MapLibre’s default)
// If you used a different encoding, set it here:
| Value | How elevation is stored | Formula to decode (pixel → meters) |
| `mapbox` (default) | 16‑bit unsigned integer split across **R** (high byte) and **G** (low byte) | `elev = ((R * 256) + G) * 0.1` |
| `terrarium` | 8‑bit per channel (R,G,B) with an offset | `elev = ((R * 256 + G) + B/256) - 32768` |
| `mapbox` (older) | Same as default, but you can force it explicitly | — |

Open the file in a browser and you’ll see a lightly shaded terrain that reacts to map pitch/rotation. Adjust the `hillshade-*` paint values until you like the visual style.

| **No hillshade appears** (just a flat gray background) | DEM source not loading (CORS, wrong URL, wrong tile format) | Open the tile URL directly in the browser → check HTTP 200 and that the image is a PNG. Ensure the server sends `Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin: *` (or your domain). |

| **Hillshade looks blocky / missing detail** | DEM tiles are low‑resolution (e.g., 512 px) or you’re zoomed in beyond the source’s max‑zoom. | Use a higher‑resolution DEM source or increase `maxzoom` in the source definition (if you host the tiles). |
| **Colors look washed out** | Default `hillshade-shadow-color` / `highlight-color` are too transparent. | Increase opacity (`rgba(0,0,0,0.8)`) or change the colors. |
| **Terrain disappears when you rotate the map** | `antialias` is `false` (default for older MapLibre versions). | Set `antialias: true` when creating the map. |

| **CORS error in console** | Your DEM tiles are on a different origin without proper CORS headers. | Add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on the tile server, or proxy the tiles through a same‑origin endpoint. |

| **Hillshade is missing on mobile Safari** | Safari requires WebGL2 for the `hillshade` layer on some devices. | Ensure you’re using MapLibre GL JS ≥ 2.4 (which falls back to a compatible shader) or set `preserveDrawingBuffer: true` as a test. |
| **Blend hillshade with a satellite raster** | Add a `raster` source for the satellite imagery, then add the hillshade **above** it and set `raster-opacity` on the satellite layer (e.g., `0.7`). |

| **Add a 3‑D terrain mesh** (extruded terrain) | Use `map.addSource('terrain', { type: 'raster-dem', ... })` **and** `map.setTerrain({ source: 'terrain', exaggeration: 1.5 })`. Hillshade will still work as a visual overlay. |
